title: Excellence Somewhere Else
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Drawing an analogy to college coaches who recruit two-sport athletes overlooked by top programs, this article argues that demonstrated excellence in any domain, not just work or school, predicts future success. It lists varied examples, from music and chess to piloting and civic leadership, as legitimate evidence of a candidate's capacity to learn, compete, and recover from setbacks. The piece recommends hiring leaders probe candidates for where they've already achieved excellence in life, treating the answer as a meaningful signal rather than a mere icebreaker. It closes by framing excellence as an acquired disposition rather than an innate skill.
points: Uses the two-sport-athlete recruiting analogy to argue excellence transfers across domains
Lists diverse examples of excellence achieved outside work or school
Recommends hiring leaders explicitly ask candidates about past achieved excellence
Frames excellence as a learned disposition, not an innate skill
quotes: Recruiting athletic talent for a Division II and III team is never easy.
High school athletes who compete successfully in two different sports possess unusual talents.
Creating excellence earlier in a career is a strong indicator of potential and learning.
Candidates who have competed and excelled in something other than work and school often incorporate insights into their work that others can’t.
Excellence doesn’t come without a host of learnings that are invaluable to succeeding elsewhere in a career and life.
The best leaders know excellence is not a skill. It is a way of learning and attitude often acquired earlier in life.
